reasoning.notes: Most decisions weigh pot odds against a range built from what the cards rule out and from opponents' earlier showdowns and bet sizes, and some reach specific, correct reads, such as calling a trailing player's 4-bet as a likely bluff. Many folds and checks only restate the score and the price, and a few range reads were wrong (the small bet read as weak was 5-5), so it falls short of 3.

evidence.quote: No other player can hold a 6, because all three copies are accounted for.
evidence.shows: Card removal used correctly to judge how strong the hand is.

evidence.quote: Seat 3 is far behind and has bluffed before: they bet 2 with [6, 1] on hand 26, which scored only 7.
evidence.shows: Uses a past showdown and the chip standings to give a 4-bet a bluff share, and calls correctly against 1-3.

evidence.quote: Seat 2 has bet 4 in each of the last few hands and taken the pot uncontested every time, so some of those bets are likely bluffs.
evidence.shows: Reads how often an opponent bets and how many pots it takes uncontested, then calls profitably with 4-4.

planning.notes: Players adjust risk to the chip standings across hands: leaders tighten and trailing players bluff more. Late in the game they plan several hands ahead, and some bluffs rest on a fold image built earlier, but most planning is endgame lead management rather than sustained multi-turn traps or set-ups.

evidence.quote: the gap drops to about 6.5, which hand 36 could realistically close.
evidence.shows: A two-hand plan that links this call to what can still be done in the last hand.

evidence.quote: My only winning path is for seat 1 to put in 4 chips and lose to me.
evidence.shows: Final-hand plan built on what an opponent must do for the bet to win the game.

evidence.quote: Both opponents folded to my BET 4 on a similar paired board in hand 9, so a large bet has a real chance of taking the pot right away.
evidence.shows: Exploits the fold image built in an earlier hand.

evidence.quote: the most anyone else can reach is 4 (seat 2 winning the pot from -2)
evidence.shows: Works out the final standings to choose a fold that guarantees at least a share of the win.

luck.notes: The hidden fourth card often turned showdowns, and margins were tiny: match 1 ended 4 to 4. The deal decided several large pots, though steals and lead protection also shaped the totals.

evidence.shows: A 6 on the last card lifted 12 to 16 and won a 9-chip pot against two 12s.

evidence.quote: I improve to 16 if the last card is a 2 or a 6.
evidence.shows: The last card hit, which turned a pot this player was behind in.

weak_spots.what: Folded 4-4 (score 14) to a 4-bet after counting that only about 13 of 78 hands beat it. Seat 3 held 3-3 (12). Calling 4 into 7 was clearly profitable, and lead protection did not justify giving up so much equity.
Called with a score of 8 after estimating its own equity at about 27%, below the 29% price it stated. Folding was the better-reasoned option.
Called with 9 on a 3-4-5 board against a first-position bettor whose shown bets were all made hands. A 9 rarely beats that range, so folding was better.

summary: Winning rewards card-removal counting, reading opponents' bet history and bet sizes, and managing chip standings near the end, but the hidden fourth card and a short 36-hand game leave much to chance. Larger bet sizes or a second betting round would make reading opponents and multi-turn planning matter more.
